主要内容: Beyond Meat and Impossible Foods are leading the alternative-meat arms race, with Burger King reporting that foot traffic for the Impossible Whopper outperformed the national average by 18.5%. McDonald's has embraced sustainable food changes, such as cage-free eggs and antibiotic-free chicken, but has not announced plans for plant-based burgers. White Castle and Little Caesars have added plant-based options, while KFC is in an exploration phase for plant-based fried chicken. Beyond Meat and Impossible Foods are expanding into nearly 20,000 restaurants, with Beyond Meat delivering a first-ever earnings report that surpassed expectations. Barclays estimates the alternative-meat market has grown to $140 billion. Consumer demand and competition are driving the shift toward plant-based protein, with Morgan Springer noting it is a matter of survival for large companies. The alternative-meat market is intensifying as major restaurant chains like TGI Fridays, Carl's Jr, Del Taco Restaurants, and Red Robin plan to offer pea- or soy-based burgers. Impossible Foods, a leader in the plant-based protein space, is struggling to meet unprecedented demand, with founder Pat Brown recruiting over 100 volunteers to work 12-hour shifts in production. The company is expanding its workforce, adding a third shift, and building a second production line in Oakland, California, while also setting up a European production arm. McDonald's CEO Easterbrook highlighted the challenge of balancing demand for alternative meat against the complexities of integrating it into restaurant kitchens. Jamie Richardson of White Castle emphasized the importance of meeting consumer preferences, particularly among Gen Z and millennials, who are increasingly interested in non-meat alternatives. The restaurant sector is also facing slower growth, prompting the need for innovation to attract customers and increase spending on higher-priced menu items. The article discusses the competition between Beyond Meat and Impossible Foods in the alternative-meat market, highlighting the shift in consumer preferences toward transparency and ethical sourcing. Margalit emphasizes that for consumers to continue viewing these products as relevant, companies must adapt to new expectations. The food industry is presented as a prime example of how generational changes can significantly impact traditional business models. Consumers now seek to know the origin of their food, its packaging, ethical raising practices, and environmental impact. The article also mentions JVP's partnership with Mars to drive foodtech innovation in Israel, reflecting the growing importance of impact alongside profit and risk in the 21st century. This trend underscores the evolving landscape of the food technology industry and its broader implications for sustainability and consumer trust.
